docs.title: groundworkers
docs.text:
groundworkers is a read-only capability layer for working with OMOP vocabularies, graph relationships, source metadata, and mapping context. It combines deterministic operations with optional embedding and model-assisted steps. It is available through three interfaces:

  • as an MCP service for discoverable tool clients
  • as a REST service for controlled workflow applications
  • as a direct Python library for in-process applications

docs.title: Choose the interface that fits your application
docs.text: Use case Recommended interface Discoverable tools or a shared remote service MCP Fixed request/response workflows, typed HTTP clients, OpenAPI REST In-process Python applications, batch evaluation, custom orchestration Direct Python

docs.title: First time setting up locally?
docs.text: Try here

docs.title: What it helps you do
docs.text:
• retrieve concepts by exact, normalized, full-text, or embedding similarity;
  • ground free text with a tiered resolver and inspect how the result was found;
  • assemble mapping evidence and graph context for review;
  • plan source artifacts before ingestion and discover applicable knowledge packs;
  • optionally normalize text, classify structured fields, or project grounded concepts into CDM rows.

Start with Concepts and capability choices for the mental model, then choose an integration path.

For agent-assisted tasks, Working with prompts explains how workflow guidance, user questions, domain knowledge, and tools fit together, and what to review before relying on a result.

Plugins explains how specialist packages extend Groundworkers, the interface they implement, and where to find the plugin catalogue and examples.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
flowchart TD PY[Python app] --> APP[build_application] MCP[MCP client] --> T[tools] REST[REST client] --> R[transports/rest] APP --> S[services/] T --> S R --> S S --> A[adapters/] A --> OG[omop-graph] A --> OE[omop-emb] A --> DB[(OMOP CDM / vocab)] A --> LLM[LLM API]
  • Services hold reusable workflow logic.
  • Adapters isolate concrete dependencies.
  • The transport layer validates input, invokes the runtime, and translates the result for its caller.
  • See Architecture for configuration and startup wiring.

docs.title: Before assuming a capability is available
docs.text:
Availability follows configuration. A CDM database enables the core vocabulary and mapping services. An embedding model plus vector store enables embedding operations. A chat model enables text preprocessing, domain classification, and assisted source planning. Semantic projection is separately opt-in.

Run this before integrating against an environment:

groundworkers --describe

The output includes the active tools, prompts, resources, plugins, redacted configuration, and safe plugin issues.

docs.title: Relationship to groundcrew
docs.text: groundworkers owns reusable stateless capabilities. groundcrew owns session state, job lifecycle, and orchestration policy. In the usual deployment, groundcrew calls Groundworkers over MCP; a Python application can use the same services directly.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: groundworkers is organised so that configuration, domain logic, and transport concerns stay separate. The same service layer is reused across MCP, REST, and direct Python integrations.

docs.title: Composition
docs.text:
The startup path is:

  1. shared OMOP stack config is loaded
  2. bootstrap.py resolves it into one runtime AppConfig
  3. build_application(...) constructs a reusable GroundworkersApp
  4. transports reuse that application container
flowchart TD STACK[StackConfig / config.toml] --> BOOT[bootstrap.py] BOOT --> CFG[AppConfig] CFG --> APP[build_application] APP --> GW[GroundworkersApp] GW --> ADP[adapters/] GW --> SVC[services/]

docs.title: Transport entry points
docs.text:
Different callers enter the same runtime in different ways:

flowchart TD MCP[MCP transport] --> TOOLS[tools/] REST[REST transport] --> API[transports/rest/] PY[Python caller] --> SVC[services/] TOOLS --> SVC TOOLS -. adapter-backed primitives .-> ADP[adapters/] API --> SVC

Most transport-facing workflows call services. MCP also exposes a small number of intentionally adapter-shaped capabilities, such as embedding and system status surfaces, where introducing a service layer would add indirection without adding domain value.

docs.title: Dependency flow
docs.text:
Services coordinate reusable domain logic. Adapters isolate concrete dependencies.

flowchart TD SVC[services/] --> ADP[adapters/] ADP --> OG[omop-graph] ADP --> OE[omop-emb] ADP --> DB[(OMOP CDM / vocab)] ADP --> LLM[LLM API]

docs.title: Shared stack configuration
docs.text:
The source of truth is the shared OMOP stack configuration loaded through oa-configurator.

  • omop-alchemy owns the CDM and vocabulary models
  • omop-graph owns graph-specific package settings
  • omop-emb owns embedding-store and embedding-model settings
  • groundworkers owns transport defaults, LLM-backed worker behavior, source-planning settings, and knowledge-pack settings

groundworkers does not maintain a second YAML-era runtime model.

docs.title: bootstrap.py
docs.text:
bootstrap.py resolves the active stack config into the runtime AppConfig. That includes:

  • selecting the active stack file
  • resolving the named CDM database and its engine
  • loading sibling package config (omop_graph, omop_emb)
  • loading groundworkers package-owned settings
  • resolving optional knowledge-pack roots

If you need to change how configuration is resolved, this is the layer to edit.

docs.title: app.py
docs.text:
build_application(config) is the composition root. It constructs:

  • adapters from already-resolved concrete handles
  • services from those adapters
  • a GroundworkersApp container that transports can reuse

This keeps the rest of the codebase free of config-file selection knowledge.

docs.title: adapters/
docs.text:
Adapters are dependency-facing wrappers. Each adapter should wrap one external system cleanly:

  • CDMAdapter wraps the SQLAlchemy engine/session factory
  • OmopGraphAdapter wraps the omop-graph backend runtime
  • OmopEmbAdapter wraps omop-emb index and query behavior
  • LLMAdapter wraps the configured model backend

Adapters are intentionally config-agnostic. They should accept already-built handles or explicit constructor values, not TOML sections or loader logic.

docs.title: services/
docs.text:
Services contain reusable domain logic that should work the same regardless of transport:

  • VocabService for lexical retrieval and OMOP navigation
  • GraphService for deterministic graph-backed lookup, traversal, paths, and neighborhood exploration
  • ConceptGroundingService for caller-facing grounding policy over the graph service
  • MappingService for multi-channel candidate and context workflows
  • TextService for LLM-backed text preprocessing
  • DomainService for LLM-backed structured-field domain hints
  • SourcePlanningService for stateless source-planning pipelines
  • SemanticProjectionService for deterministic output-definition projection over omop-semantics — grounded concept in, one or more CDM rows out

If the logic is something a Python caller would reasonably want without going through MCP, it probably belongs in a service.

Some services also depend on other services or optional adapters as part of the assembled runtime:

  • ConceptGroundingService depends on GraphService
  • MappingService depends on VocabService and can also use graph, embedding, and grounding capabilities when available
  • SourcePlanningService is always present and can be LLM-assisted when that adapter is configured

SemanticProjectionService is the one exception to the Services/adapter composition described above: it needs no adapter (no database, no LLM — the same properties that make omop-semantics itself portable), so it is not part of app.services. It's constructed directly and registered behind its own config flag, the same way KnowledgeCatalogue is. See SemanticProjectionService.

docs.title: Transport layers
docs.text:
groundworkers exposes two transport styles over the same runtime:

  • MCP via the tool modules in tools/
  • REST via transports/rest/

The transport layers should stay thin:

  1. validate or clamp request inputs
  2. call a service
  3. call an adapter directly only for intentionally adapter-shaped primitives that do not have a service abstraction
  4. translate exceptions into transport-appropriate error responses

Business logic should not exist only in MCP wrappers or only in REST routes.

docs.title: Which layer should a caller use?
docs.text: Need Call Tool discovery, agent interoperability, remote service MCP tools Fixed HTTP workflow endpoints REST API Domain workflows from Python app.services.* Backend-shaped primitives for a specific dependency app.adapters.*

docs.title: Typical request flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram participant C as Caller participant T as Transport participant S as Service participant A as Adapter participant D as Dependency C->>T: request T->>S: domain call S->>A: dependency call A->>D: query / API call D-->>A: raw result A-->>S: normalized result S-->>T: domain result T-->>C: MCP / REST / Python response

For adapter-backed MCP primitives, the T->>S and S->>A steps collapse into a direct transport-to-adapter call by design.

docs.title: Design rules for contributors
docs.text:
• Put resource resolution in bootstrap.py, not in adapters.
  • Keep adapters dependency-shaped and reusable.
  • Keep services transport-agnostic.
  • Add MCP tools only when the capability should participate in tool discovery.
  • Add REST endpoints only for curated workflow operations, not every internal method.

The extension guide in Extending groundworkers spells out the expected shape for new adapters, services, MCP tools, and REST routes.

docs.title: Concepts and capability choices
docs.text:
Groundworkers provides read-only tools for working with OMOP vocabularies and source metadata. It combines deterministic vocabulary and graph operations with optional retrieval and model-assisted steps, available through MCP, REST, or direct Python.

MCP, REST, and Python are different ways to call the same runtime. Where a service exists, they share its implementation.

docs.title: The main workflow
docs.text:
Mapping usually starts with source text or fields. Text preparation or domain classification can help narrow the search. Retrieval finds candidate concepts; grounding tries to resolve the input using ranked rules. Mapping brings the candidates, evidence, and graph context together for a caller or reviewer to choose a mapping. Optional semantic projection then uses the grounded concept and source context to produce CDM rows.

flowchart TD SOURCE["Source text or fields"] -->|Retrieval and grounding| CANDIDATES["Candidate concepts and evidence"] CANDIDATES -->|Caller or reviewer chooses| SELECTED["Selected concept or concepts"] SELECTED -. Optional semantic projection .-> ROWS["CDM rows"] SOURCE -. Source context .-> ROWS

docs.title: Retrieval
docs.text:
Retrieval asks which OMOP concepts resemble an input. Groundworkers exposes several signals:

  • exact search matches a complete concept name or synonym;
  • normalized search compares deterministic normalized text;
  • PostgreSQL full-text search matches indexed terms and returns ts_rank;
  • embedding search compares a query vector with stored concept vectors.

Use the search tools when you want to choose the strategy yourself and inspect its signals. The search results can include non-standard concepts; that is often useful because source codes and synonyms may have better lexical coverage than their standard targets.

docs.title: Grounding
docs.text:
Grounding is a ranked, policy-driven attempt to resolve free text to concepts. concept_ground runs its configured tiers in order and stops at the first tier that produces results. It reports the matched tier and whether embedding retrieval was used. Domain, vocabulary, ancestry, standardness, and activity constraints narrow the search.

flowchart TD INPUT["Text and constraints"] --> SEARCH["Search the next configured tier"] SEARCH --> MATCH{"Any matches?"} MATCH -->|Yes: stop searching| RESULT["Return candidatesand the matched tier"] MATCH -->|No| MORE{"More tiers?"} MORE -->|Yes| SEARCH MORE -->|No| EMPTY["Return no candidates"]

Grounding is not proof that the first result is the correct mapping. A caller that needs reviewable evidence should use concept_candidate_bundle, inspect the candidate union, and add concept_mapping_context for the selected concept.

docs.title: Mapping
docs.text:
Mapping is the broader decision workflow around a source term. Mapping tools combine retrieval channels, navigate non-standard concepts to standard targets, find broader standard ancestors, assemble graph context, follow Maps to value relationships, and evaluate predictions against references. They are useful when the caller must preserve evidence or ask a human or another model to make the final choice.

flowchart TD CANDIDATES["Candidates frommultiple searches"] --> REVIEW["Caller or reviewerassesses the evidence"] SOURCE["Source meaningand domain rules"] --> REVIEW GRAPH["Standard targetsand graph context"] --> REVIEW REVIEW --> DECISION["Mapping to one or more conceptswith supporting evidence"] REVIEW -->|Insufficient evidence| OPEN["Leave unresolved"]

docs.title: Deterministic and model-assisted capabilities
docs.text:
Most vocabulary and graph operations run without an LLM. Some text preparation and classification tasks use a configured model.

Capability Deterministic? Additional infrastructure Concept lookup, hierarchy, relationships, paths, and standard navigation Yes OMOP CDM/vocabulary database; graph preparation for some indexes and classified relationships Exact, normalized, and full-text retrieval Yes OMOP vocabulary database; full-text sidecars for full-text retrieval Candidate bundles and mapping context Yes, with optional embedding channel CDM and graph access; embeddings only for embedding retrieval Embedding search and embedding grounding tier Query and index operations are deterministic once vectors exist Populated embedding store plus a configured embedding model for live query encoding Text normalization, cleanup, decomposition, and disambiguation No Configured chat model with structured-output support Structured-field domain classification No Configured chat model Assisted source planning Deterministic pipeline plus optional model fallback LLM only when the assisted path is selected and configured Source planning without assistance Yes Source content and any format-specific optional extra Semantic projection Yes No database, embedding model, or LLM

An embedding model and a chat model are separate configuration references. A deployment can use embeddings without enabling chat, chat without embeddings, or neither.

docs.title: Source planning and knowledge packs
docs.text:
Source planning analyses an input before ingestion. It decomposes the input, normalizes its structure, annotates columns, and returns results such as column roles, domain hints, warnings, and an ingestion strategy. The caller manages session state and job persistence. groundcrew uses this capability.

The deterministic source_plan path uses format and header evidence. Call source_plan_assisted as a separate step when that evidence is insufficient; it can use the configured chat model. The result records whether the assisted tier was used.

Knowledge packs are a separate discovery mechanism. Bundled baseline packs and optional site or localisation packs contain reusable guidance and rules. knowledge_catalogue finds packs applicable to a source system, domain, or section; knowledge_pack loads the selected pack. Discovery can happen before or after source planning.

docs.title: Prompt guidance and user decisions
docs.text:
An agent can use workflow prompts to organise a task and elicitation prompts to ask for missing information. Domain rules and tool results help it assess the answers. Answering a question may resolve one decision while leaving other work open.

See Working with prompts for choosing guidance, handling unanswered questions, and requesting more explanation when needed.

docs.title: Semantic projection
docs.text: Grounding answers “which concept does this source item refer to?” Projection answers “given that concept and this source context, which CDM row or rows should be emitted?” It is useful for sibling-field modifiers, value-carried family history, deterministic suppression, and multi-row output definitions. Projection never chooses the concept and never calls an LLM. It must be enabled explicitly to expose the definition catalogue.

docs.title: Choose an interface
docs.text:
Choose When it fits MCP An agent needs discoverable tools, prompts, resources, and a shared remote runtime. The tool surface can vary with configuration. REST An application wants a conventional HTTP contract for the curated candidate-bundle and assisted source-planning workflows. REST is not a mirror of every MCP tool. Direct Python A Python process already owns orchestration, batching, evaluation, or review logic and should call services without a transport hop.

Use groundworkers --describe to inspect the active MCP tools, prompts, resources, and redacted runtime description. This is especially useful when optional embeddings, chat, knowledge packs, or semantic projection change what is available.

docs.title: Relationship to companion packages
docs.text:
Groundworkers uses these packages:

  • omop-alchemy provides OMOP CDM models and database configuration;
  • omop-graph provides graph-backed concept traversal and resolver primitives;
  • omop-emb provides embedding stores, indexes, and model-backed query encoding;
  • omop-semantics provides the generic output-definition runtime used by semantic projection;
  • omop-llm provides provider-neutral model backends;
  • oa-configurator resolves the shared stack configuration;
  • groundcrew owns stateful orchestration and job lifecycle, while Groundworkers provides reusable stateless capabilities.

The configuration guide explains how the shared resources are referenced. The integration guide shows the same capability layer through each transport.

docs.title: Initial local setup
docs.text:
Use this guide to connect Groundworkers to an existing OMOP CDM database and start a local service. The vocabulary tables must already be populated; Groundworkers does not load vocabulary data.

Start with the CDM connection. You can add graph indexes, embeddings, a chat model, and plugins as you need them. A chat model is not required for vocabulary lookup or lexical grounding.

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
You need Python 3.12 or newer, the database connection details, and access to the CDM and vocabulary schemas. If the vocabulary is stored separately from the clinical tables, configure its connection and schema too.

The setup console helps you edit configuration, test connections, and run preparation tasks. It does not run your agent conversations or mapping jobs. Configuration is saved to a shared TOML file; maintenance runs have their own saved history. Connection and model checks may need to be rerun after reopening the console or changing a service.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
In a new working directory, create and activate a virtual environment. These activation commands are for macOS and Linux:

uv venv --python 3.12
source .venv/bin/activate

Install Groundworkers with the setup console:

uv pip install "groundworkers[tui]"

If you plan to store embeddings in PostgreSQL, include its backend support:

uv pip install "groundworkers[tui,embedding-pgvector]"

Other extras include embedding-faiss for FAISS sidecar acceleration and all_source for XLSX, PDF, and DOCX source-planning inputs. See Installation for the available extras.

docs.title: 2. Open the setup console
docs.text:
groundworkers tui

The default configuration file is ~/.config/omop/config.toml, unless OA_CONFIG_PATH selects another file. To choose a file explicitly:

groundworkers tui --config-path /path/to/config.toml

The console can help you choose a location and create or repair the configuration. Review the redacted diff before applying changes. Use the same configuration path when you later start the service.

Overview shows CDM readiness separately from optional graph, embedding, chat, and integration status. An unconfigured optional feature does not mean the CDM service has failed.

docs.title: 3. Configure the CDM
docs.text:
Choose Overview → Configure CDM, or open Database. Configure the physical connection and the logical CDM database, including the vocabulary location. The setup flow writes the shared [connections.*], [databases.*], and [tools.groundworkers] entries. Groundworkers refers to these entries by name.

Run Test connections in Database or Verify all in Overview. A working CDM connection with populated vocabulary tables supports concept lookup, lexical search and grounding, and mapping tools. Some searches and graph operations also need the preparation described below.

See Configuration for the shared configuration layout and named references.

docs.title: 4. Prepare graph and search support
docs.text:
Open Graph → Prepare graph when readiness reports missing relationship, full-text, or functional indexes. Review the proposed commands before starting. Performance shows index readiness and offers further index maintenance.

Preparation runs as a background maintenance task; follow it in Runs. The database account used for preparation needs permission to create the required indexes and supporting objects. Normal service queries remain read-only.

You can use basic vocabulary operations before preparing every index. Prepare the search and graph support needed by the tools you intend to use, then rerun the checks.

docs.title: 5. Add embeddings (optional)
docs.text:
Embedding search needs a named embedding model, a named vector store, and vectors for the concepts you want to search. The query model must be compatible with the stored vectors.

  1. Configure the store. Use Database to select or create the vector-store configuration.
  2. Configure the model. In Embeddings, choose Configure model. Supply the provider details and select a model already registered in the store or a new model from the provider.
  3. Initialize and check. Use Initialize embedding store if needed, then Check model to check the store registration and test whether the provider can encode text with that model.
  4. Choose the scope and populate. Refresh coverage, select the vocabularies you need, and choose Populate. Review the scope, run limit, and commands before starting.
  5. Check the result. Follow the task in Runs, then refresh coverage to see what is available.

Store initialization and population write to the embedding store. Population starts only when requested; a search never triggers it. A run limit caps the amount of work in one run. Coverage and the population plan show which concepts still need vectors.

An embedding model and a chat model are separate choices and can use different providers. Configuring one does not enable the other.

docs.title: 6. Add a chat model (optional)
docs.text:
Open Chat Model, configure the provider, and run Test provider. Use Select chat model to choose a model that supports structured output. The separate Chat section checks the selected model's chat and structured-output capabilities.

Chat enables text preparation and structured-field domain classification. Assisted source planning also needs source_planning_llm_assisted_enabled to be enabled; it is enabled by default. Provider support comes from omop-llm; use the console checks to verify your chosen endpoint and model. Credentials are redacted in configuration reviews and diagnostics.

docs.title: 7. Start or inspect the service
docs.text:
After setup, inspect what Groundworkers will expose for your configuration:

groundworkers --config-path /path/to/config.toml --describe

This lists registered tools, prompts, resources, plugins, and redacted configuration details. Use the console's connection and model checks to verify that the configured services are reachable too.

For an agent client that launches Groundworkers, use MCP over stdio:

groundworkers --config-path /path/to/config.toml --transport stdio

To run an MCP service that clients can connect to over HTTP:

groundworkers \
  --config-path /path/to/config.toml \
  --transport streamable-http \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8000

REST runs as a separate transport, with selected mapping and source-planning endpoints:

groundworkers \
  --config-path /path/to/config.toml \
  --transport rest \
  --host 127.0.0.1 \
  --port 8080

These HTTP examples listen on the local machine. See Integrations for client setup and the available interfaces. Restart a running service after changing its configuration or installed plugins.

docs.title: Optional plugins and guidance
docs.text:
Installed Groundworkers plugins can add tools, prompts, resources, and setup pages. Install them into the same Python environment as Groundworkers, then reopen the console or restart the service. Use --describe to check what was registered; plugins with readiness support also report configuration or dependency problems in the console.

For prompt packs, see Working with prompts. Bundled knowledge packs are available without a separate plugin; local knowledge-pack paths and the optional semantic_projection_enabled setting are described in Configuration.

docs.title: Configuration managed elsewhere
docs.text:
To inspect a deployment-managed or copied configuration without editing it:

groundworkers tui \
  --config-path /path/to/config.toml \
  --config-read-only

Change the authoritative configuration source, then reopen the console to verify the result. This flag disables configuration edits; it does not make database preparation tasks read-only.

docs.title: Maintenance runs
docs.text:
Graph preparation and embedding population run in separate background processes. You can close and reopen the console while they continue. In Runs, follow progress, inspect a redacted log tail, cancel active work, retry a supported failed step, or export commands. Postflight results appear for tasks that define those checks.

Run history is saved on disk. Groundworkers uses GROUNDWORKERS_STATE_HOME, then XDG_STATE_HOME, as the state base directory and appends groundworkers. If neither is set, it uses ~/.local/state/groundworkers.

In a container, set the state base to a mounted persistent directory to retain history across container replacement. An interrupted worker does not resume merely because its history survives; inspect its status in Runs before retrying.

docs.title: Plugins
docs.text:
Plugins add specialist capabilities to a Groundworkers installation. A plugin can expose tools, prompts, and resources through the same MCP server as the core vocabulary and mapping tools. It can also provide configuration pages, readiness checks, and preparation tasks in the setup console.

Start with the Groundworkers Plugin Catalogue to find components, installation instructions, and compatibility information. Access to the catalogue or individual component repositories may be required. Each component's own guide explains its data requirements and intended use.

docs.title: What gets installed
docs.text:
The ecosystem includes both executable plugins and reusable prompt content:

Component How it fits Runtime plugin A Python package that Groundworkers discovers and asks to register its MCP capabilities. Installed prompt pack A content distribution read by the OHDSI Prompt Registry plugin. It supplies instructions, schemas, or examples. Filesystem prompt pack Content read by the registry from a configured directory, often for local guidance or a working copy.

For example, installing the Prompt Registry adds tools for finding and reading packs. Adding a pack supplies content to those tools. A pack does not need to implement the Groundworkers plugin interface itself.

The catalogue describes what you can install. Your Python environment determines what Groundworkers can discover. Configuration and available dependencies determine which capabilities can be built and used.

docs.title: How a plugin joins the host
docs.text:
A plugin package advertises a constructed plugin object through the groundworkers.plugins Python entry-point group. Groundworkers discovers that object at startup, supplies its configuration and shared resources, and asks it to build its state. It then registers the plugin's MCP tools, prompts, or resources against that state.

flowchart TD PACKAGE["Installed plugin package"] --> BUILD["Build plugin state"] HOST["Groundworkers resourcesand plugin settings"] --> BUILD BUILD --> MCP["Register tools, prompts and resourceson the shared MCP server"]

The plugin's service contains its own behaviour. Groundworkers provides discovery, shared runtime access, MCP registration, and common setup features. Registering MCP capabilities does not automatically create REST endpoints; REST exposes a separate set of workflows.

docs.title: The interface contract
docs.text:
Every runtime plugin implements four parts:

Part Responsibility name A stable identity, unique among installed plugins. config_cls The plugin's configuration schema, or None when no settings are needed. Its tool_name must match the plugin name. build(context, config) Use shared resources and validated plugin settings to create the state needed by the plugin. Return None if a required prerequisite is missing. register(server, state) Expose MCP tools, prompts, or resources using the state returned by build.

The supplied PluginContext gives a plugin access to resolved CDM resources, the routed CDM session factory, and optional embedding, chat, and mapping capabilities. A plugin can reuse the host's grounding and mapping through mapping_context. Routed CDM sessions support installations where vocabulary tables use a different connection from clinical tables.

Plugins can also declare references to independent databases, models, or vector stores. Their settings belong in [tools.<plugin_name>]; connection details and credentials stay in the shared resource entries they reference. See Configuration for how these settings fit into the stack.

A plugin can optionally add:

  • Readiness checks to distinguish valid settings from usable data and services.
  • Setup steps for explicit preparation work, with progress and logs in Runs.
  • A custom configuration flow when its settings need more than the standard generated form.

An individual plugin can be skipped when its configuration, prerequisites, build, or registration fail, while core capabilities remain available. Plugin identities must still be unique: duplicate names are a startup error. MCP tool names also share a namespace, so plugins should prefix their tool names.

For method signatures, entry-point declarations, and authoring details, see the plugin development guide.

docs.title: OHDSI Prompt Registry: exposing reusable guidance
docs.text:
The OHDSI Prompt Registry is a runtime plugin that publishes prompt packs through MCP. Its tools let an agent discover packs, read selected instructions or schemas, validate structured documents, and render supported results for review.

The registry can combine bundled content, separately installed pack distributions, and local filesystem packs. This lets a team share a workflow while keeping site-specific content separately maintained. Your agent conducts the conversation and applies the guidance; the registry supplies content and contract checks.

See Working with prompts for the user-facing model and the registry's pack-source guide for configuration.

docs.title: Plugin template: a small service with tools and setup
docs.text:
The Groundworkers Plugin Template provides a small catalogue service with list, search, and status tools. It also demonstrates a preparation step and a readiness report. It is a starting point for authors to adapt.

Its layout shows where the responsibilities belong:

Module Purpose config.py Declare settings and references to shared resources. adapters.py Read files, query databases, or call external services. service.py Implement behaviour that can also be called directly from Python. tools.py Expose that behaviour through MCP. plugin.py Build the components and register the plugin's capabilities.

Longer preparation work lives separately in setup_cli.py and can run through the host's maintenance system. A specialised mapper can follow the same structure, reusing Groundworkers' mapping context while keeping source-specific rules and data in its own package.

docs.title: Add a plugin to your installation
docs.text:
1. Check compatibility. Use the catalogue to find the component's requirements, installation command, and recorded test evidence. A declared version range and a successful compatibility test are different kinds of evidence.
  2. Install and configure it. Use the same Python environment that runs Groundworkers. Follow the component's guide for settings and any data preparation, then restart the host.
  3. Inspect the result. Check registration and use the plugin's readiness checks, where available, to verify its dependencies and prepared data.
groundworkers --config-path /path/to/config.toml --describe

The output lists active plugins and registered capabilities, with safe issue summaries for plugins that could not be built or registered. A registered tool may still need a working connection or prepared data before a call succeeds.

docs.title: CDM Adapter
docs.text: CDMAdapter holds the primary engine, vocabulary engine, and routed session factory for a resolved CDM database. It is the shared connection layer used by VocabService and OmopGraphAdapter.

docs.title: What it is
docs.text:
CDMAdapter is a thin connection-management object. It does not issue queries itself. Its purpose is to:

  • hold the primary and vocabulary sqlalchemy.Engine objects
  • expose a routed session factory for callers that query role-tagged OMOP tables
  • be constructed once per CDM database in build_application() and shared across the components that need it

docs.title: Who uses it
docs.text:
Component How VocabService Takes a CDMAdapter as its only constructor argument. Uses the session factory to open per-call sessions for vocabulary table queries. OmopGraphAdapter Uses the routed session factory so vocabulary and primary-role graph tables reach their configured databases.

The adapter is created once per CDM database at application startup and wired through build_application(). It is not per-request.

docs.title: Construction
docs.text:
CDMAdapter is config-agnostic. It accepts an engine and optional routed factory, while build_application() creates them through omop_alchemy.config.create_cdm_engines() and omop_alchemy.cross_database.cdm_sessionmaker():

  • the adapter remains testable by passing a SQLite engine directly
  • changing the connection source means changing build_application() only;CDMAdapter and every service that uses it are untouched

docs.title: Usage from build_application()
docs.text:
from groundworkers.app import build_application
from groundworkers.bootstrap import build_app_config

config = build_app_config()
app = build_application(config)

# CDMAdapter is available at:
app.adapters.cdm

VocabService is wired automatically: 

app.services.vocab  # backed by app.adapters.cdm

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
build_app_config() creates role engines through create_cdm_engines(..., register_claims=False). Startup fails fast when either database role is unreachable and prints the scrubbed reason with a database recovery hint. CDMAdapter.is_available() also performs a lightweight Core query (SELECT 1).

close() disposes both role engines. Call it explicitly in teardown (for example in a test fixture yield/finally block) when you need to ensure connections are returned promptly. Process-level startup and shutdown wiring belongs in the application or transport layer, not in the adapter itself.

docs.title: OmopEmb Adapter
docs.text: OmopEmbAdapter wraps omop-emb for embedding-backed concept retrieval.

docs.title: What it owns
docs.text:
The adapter is responsible for:

  • nearest-neighbour lookup against the configured embedding store
  • optional on-the-fly query encoding through an embedding client
  • exposing backend availability and registered model metadata

The adapter does not resolve stack config itself. build_application(...) constructs it from Groundworkers' [tools.groundworkers] embedding_model_name and vector_store_name references.

docs.title: Backends
docs.text:
groundworkers supports the same primary storage backends it wires from omop-emb:

Backend Groundworkers stack config sqlitevec a [vector_stores.*] entry with backend_type = "sqlitevec" and a database reference pgvector a [vector_stores.*] entry with backend_type = "pgvector" and a database reference

FAISS remains a sidecar acceleration layer rather than a standalone primary backend.

docs.title: Index lookup mode
docs.text:
No live model API is required.

  • embedding_neighbours reads an existing concept vector from the index
  • index_status reports registered models and concept counts

docs.title: Text search mode
docs.text:
Requires embedding_model_name and vector_store_name, plus a configured embedding provider/model.

  • embedding_search encodes a text query on the fly
  • embedding_search_batch encodes and searches multiple text queries with one provider/index batch, returning rows aligned to input order
  • embedding_encode returns a raw embedding vector

docs.title: Availability model
docs.text:
The underlying backend is built lazily on first use. If the backend cannot be opened, the adapter reports unavailability rather than failing application construction for callers that do not need embedding-backed operations.

Representative index_status() shape:

{
  "available": true,
  "backend_type": "pgvector",
  "models": [
    {
      "model_name": "qwen3-embedding:0.6b",
      "provider": "OLLAMA",
      "dimensions": 1024,
      "index_type": "FLAT",
      "concept_count": 438924
    }
  ]
}

docs.title: Where it is used
docs.text:
• embedding MCP tools
  • the embedding channel inside MappingService.concept_candidate_bundle(...)
  • optional embedding-tier support inside graph grounding when an embedding client is successfully wired into OmopGraphAdapter

docs.title: OmopGraph Adapter
docs.text: OmopGraphAdapter wraps omop-graph as the backend runtime for graph-backed concept operations. It owns the dependency-shaped interface to omop-graph; caller-facing graph workflows live one layer up in GraphService and ConceptGroundingService.

docs.title: What it owns
docs.text:
The adapter is responsible for:

  • building and probing the omop-graph runtime lazily
  • normalizing raw concept and graph results into plain Python dicts and tuples
  • translating backend failures into GroundworkersError
  • exposing one-operation primitives that services can compose into higher-level workflows

It does not own caller-facing policy such as hierarchy-walk packaging, grounding tier selection, or REST/MCP response shaping.

docs.title: Primitive surface
docs.text:
Method Used by service(s) get_concept(concept_id) GraphService get_concept_by_code(vocab, code) GraphService concept_views(concept_ids) GraphService parents(concept_id) / children(concept_id) GraphService edges(concept_id, ...) GraphService shortest_paths(source_id, target_id, ...) GraphService traverse_neighborhood(concept_id, ...) GraphService run_ground_tier(resolvers, query, ...) GraphService grounding orchestration get_vocabulary_catalogue() system_vocabulary_catalogue canonicalize_domain(domain) ConceptGroundingService embedding_resolver_active ConceptGroundingService is_available() system_status probe() system_status

VocabService uses CDMAdapter for lexical search operations and is separate from the omop-graph-backed graph service surface.

docs.title: Concept response shape
docs.text:
All methods that return concept data use a consistent dict shape:

{
  "concept_id": 4119419,
  "concept_name": "Malignant neoplasm of bronchus and lung",
  "concept_code": "363358000",
  "vocabulary_id": "SNOMED",
  "domain_id": "Condition",
  "concept_class_id": "Clinical Finding",
  "standard_concept": true,
  "valid_start_date": "2002-01-31",
  "valid_end_date": "2099-12-31",
  "invalid_reason": null
}

standard_concept is a boolean (true/false), not the raw "S" / null string stored in the OMOP CDM.

docs.title: Full-text search
docs.text:
ConceptGroundingService runs a tiered resolver pipeline through this adapter. The FullText tier uses PostgreSQL tsvector sidecar columns (concept_name_tsvector, concept_synonym_name_tsvector) when they are present on the vocabulary tables. Detection is automatic. When the sidecar columns are absent, the FullText tier returns no results and the pipeline falls through to later tiers.

concept_search_fulltext (via VocabService) uses the same sidecar columns and exposes tsvector_available so callers can detect degraded mode.

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Adapter methods raise GroundworkersError on failure. Services propagate those errors unchanged; tools and REST routes translate them into transport-level responses.

The underlying KnowledgeGraph is built lazily on first use rather than at server startup. If the database or graph layer is unavailable, callers receive a clear GroundworkersError instead of an opaque lower-level exception.

docs.title: Extending groundworkers
docs.text:
This guide is for contributors adding new adapters, services, MCP tools, or REST endpoints directly in this repository. If you're adding a self-contained capability as a separate installable package instead — no core file edits — see Plugin architecture. The main rule here is simple:

keep business logic above the transport layer and keep dependency details below it.

docs.title: Current extension points
docs.text: If you are adding... Put it in... A wrapper around one external dependency src/groundworkers/adapters/ Reusable domain logic coordinating adapters src/groundworkers/services/ An MCP tool surface src/groundworkers/tools/ A curated HTTP route src/groundworkers/transports/rest/ Runtime config resolution src/groundworkers/bootstrap.py Package-owned config fields src/groundworkers/config.py

docs.title: Adding a new adapter
docs.text:
Use an adapter when the main job is to wrap one external system cleanly.

Adapter expectations:

  • accept already-resolved handles or explicit constructor values
  • do not read TOML or environment variables directly
  • expose dependency-shaped operations with predictable Python errors
  • raise GroundworkersError for backend-facing failures that callers should reason about

Good adapter candidates:

  • a new OMOP-adjacent query layer
  • a new read-only store for reusable knowledge
  • a new model backend wrapper

Poor adapter candidates:

  • transport-specific request parsing
  • orchestration across multiple dependencies
  • policy about when a caller should prefer one retrieval strategy over another

docs.title: Adding a new service
docs.text:
Use a service when the capability contains reusable domain logic that a Python caller should be able to use directly.

Service expectations:

  • be transport-agnostic
  • coordinate one or more adapters
  • hold workflow logic, scoring, routing, or packaging behavior
  • return normal Python results, not MCP-style error dicts

Typical pattern:

  1. add or extend the adapter operations you need
  2. add the domain logic in services/
  3. wire the service in build_application(...)
  4. expose it through MCP or REST only if the capability should be transported

docs.title: Adding an MCP tool
docs.text:
Add an MCP tool when the capability should participate in tool discovery or be available to remote clients.

Tool expectations:

  1. validate and clamp inputs
  2. call a service
  3. call an adapter directly only when the capability is intentionally adapter-shaped and there is no service abstraction
  4. translate exceptions into MCP-safe error dicts

Do not put the main business logic in the tool wrapper itself.

docs.title: Adding a REST endpoint
docs.text:
REST is curated. Do not mirror every MCP tool automatically.

Add a REST route when:

  • the workflow has a stable request/response contract
  • a typed HTTP client is a likely consumer
  • the route is better understood as an application operation than as a generic tool

Route expectations:

  • request and response models live in transports/rest/models.py
  • routes call services directly, not MCP wrappers
  • transport-specific error mapping stays in transports/rest/api.py

docs.title: Updating configuration
docs.text:
Before adding a new config field, decide which package actually owns that concern.

Use this rough split:

  • omop-alchemy: CDM and vocabulary models
  • omop-graph: graph traversal behavior
  • omop-emb: embedding store and embedding model settings
  • groundworkers: transport defaults, LLM worker behavior, source-planning behavior, knowledge-pack behavior

If the setting belongs to groundworkers, add it to GroundworkersConfig in config.py and let bootstrap.py thread it into the runtime.

docs.title: Testing new capabilities
docs.text:
Preferred test seams:

  • use build_app_config_from_stack(...) for runtime bootstrap tests
  • unit-test services with fake adapters where practical
  • test MCP registration through create_server(...)
  • test REST routes with fastapi.testclient.TestClient

The goal is to keep each layer testable without needing the full deployment stack.

docs.title: Practical checklist
docs.text:
When a new capability is ready, check:

  • config resolution happens in bootstrap.py, not in the adapter
  • the adapter is config-agnostic
  • the service is transport-agnostic
  • MCP and REST wrappers stay thin
  • docs describe the current interface and a real use case

docs.title: Integrating groundworkers
docs.text: How to drive Groundworkers from Python against the same steady-state configuration the setup console produces. Nothing here imports Textual, Groundskeeping, or another application's setup code.

docs.title: Build the runtime
docs.text:
from groundworkers.app import build_application
from groundworkers.bootstrap import build_app_config

config = build_app_config(config_path="/path/to/config.toml")
app = build_application(config)

build_app_config resolves the stack and returns an AppConfig holding only Groundworkers-owned values:

Attribute Type groundworkers GroundworkersConfig cdm_database ResolvedCDMDatabase cdm_engine, cdm_vocab_engine sqlalchemy.Engine cdm_session_factory Routed SQLAlchemy session factory for primary, vocabulary, and results roles embedding_model ResolvedModel \| None vector_store ResolvedVectorStore \| None

Omitting config_path uses OA_CONFIG_PATH or the default stack location.

docs.title: Available services
docs.text:
app.services attributes are None only when their prerequisites are absent, so check before use:

services = app.services

services.vocab          # always, with a CDM database
services.graph          # always, with a CDM database
services.grounding      # always, with a CDM database
services.mapping        # always, with a CDM database
services.text           # only when groundworkers.llm_model_name resolves
services.domain         # only when groundworkers.llm_model_name resolves
services.source_planning

A CDM-only configuration is fully supported. Graph availability follows the resolved CDM database — there is no separate section to enable.

The engines are created by omop_alchemy.config.create_cdm_engines(..., register_claims=False), and cdm_session_factory comes from omop_alchemy.cross_database.cdm_sessionmaker. Use the session factory for queries that may touch more than one OMOP role. On PostgreSQL, engine creation checks role schema claims eagerly, so the configured databases must be reachable while build_app_config() runs.

docs.title: Grounding free text
docs.text:
result = app.services.grounding.ground(
    "type 2 diabetes",
    limit=10,
    domain="Condition",
    vocabulary_id=None,
    parent_ids=None,        # optional required-ancestor constraint
    standard_only=False,    # narrows candidate resolution, not results
    active_only=False,
)

for hit in result["results"]:
    if hit["standard_concept"]:
        print(hit["concept_id"], hit["concept_name"])
    elif hit["classification_concept"]:
        # A real hierarchy node, but not a valid CDM entity-field target.
        print("classification:", hit["concept_id"], hit["concept_name"])

limit must be positive; a non-positive value raises GroundworkersError with code INVALID_INPUT.

docs.title: Interpreting the explanation
docs.text:
explanation = result["grounding_explanation"]
explanation["matched_tier"]           # EXACT | FULLTEXT | EMBEDDING_NEAREST | PARTIAL
explanation["used_embedding"]         # bool
explanation["embedding_tier_detail"]  # None, or why the embedding tier was skipped

Tiers run in order and the first one that yields results wins. When embedding_tier_detail is set, the embedding tier was planned but could not run — usually an unreachable provider — and the answer came from lexical tiers alone. Treat a set value as "this result may be incomplete".

docs.title: Error handling
docs.text:
Every service raises GroundworkersError with a stable code:

from groundworkers.base.errors import GroundworkersError

try:
    concept = app.services.graph.get_concept(201826)
except GroundworkersError as exc:
    print(exc.code, exc.message)   # NOT_FOUND | INVALID_INPUT | BACKEND_UNAVAIL | QUERY_ERROR | …

Messages are safe to log and surface: provider and database failures are translated so they do not carry credentials or connection strings.

docs.title: Concept flag contract
docs.text:
Field Meaning standard_concept true only for raw standard_concept = 'S' classification_concept true only for raw standard_concept = 'C' is_active invalid_reason unset, treating blank and whitespace-only as active

Do not derive standardness from omop-graph's ConceptView.standard_concept: that field is a single boolean covering both 'S' and 'C'. Groundworkers reads the raw flag at its adapter boundary so callers get the distinction.

docs.title: Writing configuration
docs.text:
Configuration writes are a local console concern, not part of the integration surface. If you are embedding the setup console in another host application, drive GroundworkersConfigMutationService through Groundskeeping's ConfigWizardController:

from groundskeeping.configurator import ConfigWizardController, MutationOperation

from groundworkers.application.setup.configuration_provider import (
    CDM_SETUP_TARGET,
    GroundworkersConfigMutationService,
    cdm_setup_workflow,
)
from groundworkers.application.setup.model_inventory import discover_provider_models

service = GroundworkersConfigMutationService(
    "/path/to/config.toml",
    model_discoverer=discover_provider_models,
)
operation = (
    MutationOperation.UPDATE
    if service.capabilities(CDM_SETUP_TARGET, MutationOperation.UPDATE).supported
    else MutationOperation.CREATE
)
controller = ConfigWizardController(cdm_setup_workflow(operation), service)

The same shape covers MODEL_SETUP_TARGET / model_setup_workflow, LLM_SETUP_TARGET / llm_setup_workflow, and VECTOR_STORE_SETUP_TARGET / vector_store_setup_workflow. The provider decides create-versus-update from the current file, owns revision checking and redaction, and returns conflicted rather than clobbering another writer. model_discoverer is the injected seam for live model inventory; supply your own to avoid network calls in tests.

This requires the tui extra for Groundskeeping, but not Textual — the provider and controller are host-agnostic.

docs.title: Plugin architecture
docs.text: For an overview and examples, start with Plugins. This guide covers the implementation contract for plugin authors.

docs.title: What a plugin is
docs.text:
Groundworkers plugins are independently installed packages that add an adapter, service, and MCP surface without adding plugin-specific imports to Groundworkers. They register one ready-to-use plugin object under the groundworkers.plugins entry-point group.

[project.entry-points."groundworkers.plugins"]
my_plugin = "my_package.plugin:plugin"
flowchart LR subgraph PKG["my_package — a separate installed package"] direction TB CFG["Config classthe settings this plugin needs"] OBJ["Plugin objectname · config class · build() · register()"] end subgraph HOST["Groundworkers — the host application"] direction TB DISC["Discoverylooks up installed plugins"] CTX["Shared connectionsdatabase, embeddings — alreadyset up by Groundworkers itself"] SRV["Shared MCP tool server"] end OBJ -.->|"found via the environment'sown package listing"| DISC DISC -->|"reads + validates"| CFG CTX -->|"handed to"| OBJ OBJ -->|"register() adds its tools"| SRV

The object implements GroundworkersPlugin: a stable name, an optional PackageConfigBase class, build(context, config), and register(server, state). The plugin name and config_cls.tool_name must match. Installed plugin names must be unique.

class MyPlugin:
    name = "my_plugin"
    config_cls = ExampleConfig  # or None, if this plugin needs no configuration

    def build(self, context, config):
        ...  # return a service object, or None if a prerequisite is unavailable

    def register(self, server, state):
        ...  # add this plugin's MCP tools/resources


plugin = MyPlugin()

docs.title: Start from the use case
docs.text:
A plugin's configuration should follow from what it needs to be able to complete its task.

Work through each requirement before writing the class.

For example, a plugin recommending comparator cohorts might reason like this.

Reuse a resource Groundworkers already resolved. Nothing to declare — read it straight off PluginContext inside build():

Use case What you need How you get it Look up existing OMOP concepts Read access through Groundworkers' routed vocabulary session context.cdm_session_factory / context.resolver Rank or filter by similarity to concepts Groundworkers already embedded The concept embeddings Groundworkers already populated, via omop-emb context.vector_store + context.embedding_backend_factory Ask an LLM to help decide something The chat model Groundworkers already configured, via omop-llm context.chat_backend_factory

Create something this plugin owns. Each becomes a field on its own PackageConfigBase — see Package configuration:

Use case What you need Configuration field established Notes Store its own distinct non-CDM source tables A database connection this plugin owns and writes to comparator_db: Annotated[str, RefTo(CDMDatabaseConfig)] = "cdm_db" Same shape as a core reference, but the operator points it at a new entry when they configure the plugin Vectorised arbitrary free text or objects for similarity search Its own embedding model embedding_model_name: Annotated[str \| None, RefTo(ModelConfig)] = None Optional, independent of Groundworkers' own model choice Store and search those vectors Its own vector index vector_store_name: Annotated[str \| None, RefTo(VectorStoreConfig)] = None Not existing OMOP concepts, see above Let operators tune how strict "similar enough" is Parameter the plugin's logic requires min_databases_default: int = Field(default=2, ge=1) A plain setting, nothing to resolve

The concept-embedding row and the free-text-embedding row look similar but are not the same decision: the first reuses a vector store Groundworkers already populated with OMOP concepts; the second stands up an independent embedding model and vector store for data that was never a concept to begin with. Reusing context.vector_store for the second case would put unrelated vectors in Groundworkers' own concept index.

docs.title: Assumptions this table is making
docs.text:
• Vocabulary only, so far. Every example above reads OMOP vocabulary: concepts, concept relationships, concept embeddings, or the host's shared grounding cascade. context.cdm_session_factory routes vocabulary and primary roles, including on split-vocabulary deployments. Clinical/person-level queries need a database role explicitly configured for them.
  • Shared mapping access. PluginContext.mapping_context is an optional,read-only capability façade over the host's mapping and grounding policy. Use its operations when a plugin needs candidate bundles, text grounding, or concept context. concept_shared_standard_ancestor(concept_ids, max_depth=5) returns the unique nearest shared standard ancestor when one exists; raise max_depth to widen the hierarchy search. The underlying vocabulary, graph, and service objects are deliberately not exposed. Do not construct a second omop-graph or vocabulary adapter from context.cdm_engine. The field is None only when the host did not compose services for the plugin context.

docs.title: Build and register a new plugin
docs.text:
build() receives PluginContext. The context provides the resolved CDM database and primary engine, routed cdm_session_factory, vocabulary engine, vector store, shared lazy model backend factories, the optional read-only mapping_context, and a deliberately narrow resolver for independent named OA resources. Return None when a prerequisite is unavailable. Groundworkers then keeps serving its core capabilities and reports why the plugin was not activated.

Use context.cdm_session_factory for role-tagged OMOP queries. context.cdm_engine remains available for primary-role access. On split-vocabulary stacks, plugins must use the routed factory; an Engine-based OmopGraphAdapter or DomainNameResolver cannot route vocabulary queries and will fail with upgrade guidance.

register() adds MCP tools, prompts, or resources against the state returned by build(). The shared MCP registration wrapper supplies the same safe error translation used by core tools. Code-defined prompts can continue to derive their arguments from the callable signature. A plugin publishing data-defined prompts can pass explicit string metadata with PromptArgument; this keeps dynamic pack fields out of Python closure signatures:

from groundworkers.base import PromptArgument

server.prompt(
    "my_pack_workflow",
    title="Run my pack workflow",
    description="Start the workflow published by my pack.",
    arguments=[
        PromptArgument(
            "request",
            "The user's starting request.",
            required=False,
        )
    ],
)(handler)
sequenceDiagram participant Env as Installed packages participant GW as Groundworkers (host) participant P as my_package (a plugin) Note over Env: 1. GW->>Env: At startup: list every registered plugin Env-->>GW: my_package's plugin object Note over GW,P: 2. GW->>P: Resolve its config class into validated settings GW->>P: build(shared connections, those settings) P-->>GW: its own service object (or "not available") GW->>P: register(shared MCP server, that service object) P-->>GW: adds its own tools to the shared server Note over GW: 3.
  1. The plugin's own installer registered one entry: "here is my plugin object."
  2. Groundworkers' code never imports my_package by name. It only expects four things on the object (name, optional PackageConfigBase class, plus build and register methods, described above).
  3. The plugin's tools are now callable through the one Groundworkers server.

docs.title: Package configuration
docs.text:
A plugin with scalar and RefTo fields receives a setup-console page without any Groundskeeping-aware plugin code:

from typing import Annotated, ClassVar

from oa_configurator import CDMDatabaseConfig, PackageConfigBase, RefTo
from pydantic import Field


class ExampleConfig(PackageConfigBase):
    tool_name: ClassVar[str] = "my_plugin"

    database: Annotated[str, RefTo(CDMDatabaseConfig)] = "cdm_db"
    retries: int = Field(default=2, ge=1)

The generic workflow maps supported Pydantic scalars to Groundskeeping fields, offers existing references of the correct concrete type, and can create a new reference chain recursively through oa-configurator's public plan_configure() API. Candidates remain private to the Groundworkers provider; review output is redacted and persistence is revision-aware.

Schemas requiring live discovery or a conditional flow (and therefore not fitting the default configuration UX specification) may additionally implement the runtime-checkable GroundworkersPluginConfigUI protocol. Its tui_workflow(operation) method returns a custom (ConfigWorkflowSpec, ConfigMutationService) pair. Keep Groundskeeping in the plugin's optional TUI dependencies so headless plugin imports remain lightweight.

docs.title: Sensitive fields
docs.text:
PackageConfigBase inherits oa-configurator's SecretSafeModel. A plugin developer must mark every plugin-owned secret with Sensitive() so model representations, interactive fields, configuration views, and review diffs can redact it by schema declaration. Groundworkers does not infer sensitivity from field names.

from typing import Annotated, ClassVar

from oa_configurator import PackageConfigBase
from oa_configurator.refs import Sensitive, Secret
from pydantic import Field


class ExampleConfig(PackageConfigBase):
    tool_name: ClassVar[str] = "my_plugin"
    api_token: Annotated[str | None, Sensitive()] = Field(default=None)

The Secret alias is equivalent to Annotated[str | None, Sensitive()]. Prefer a RefTo field when a plugin can reuse an existing database, model, provider, or vector-store entry. The plugin then stores only the logical reference name; sensitivity remains declared on the referenced schema, such as ConnectionConfig.password or ProviderConfig.api_key, and the generic recursive configuration workflow preserves those declarations.

This protects display and logging surfaces; it does not encrypt persisted configuration. Plugin documentation must describe the storage expectations for any secret it introduces.

docs.title: Upgrading plugins to Groundworkers 0.7
docs.text:
1. Require oa-configurator>=2,<3 and groundworkers>=0.7,<0.8 in the plugin package.
  2. Import Sensitive and Secret from oa_configurator.refs, and load files with load_stack_config(path).
  3. Create CDM role engines with omop_alchemy.config.create_cdm_engines(resolved, register_claims=False) for read-only plugin access; use context.cdm_session_factory when Groundworkers provides the database.
  4. Remove schema fields from SQLite database entries. For PostgreSQL CDM entries, use cdm_schema; vector-store database entries continue to use schema_name.
  5. Keep accepting context.cdm_engine for integrations that need the primary SQLAlchemy engine. The routed factory handles vocabulary, primary, and results roles for ORM queries.
  6. Treat context.embedding_backend_factory() as a read-only omop-emb 3.0 EmbeddingStoreReader. It is shared with Groundworkers tools and status; reader methods no longer accept metric_type, and model enumeration is get_registered_models(). Do not use it to register models, create tables, or write vectors. Use a plugin-owned store and explicit setup operation for plugin data.
  7. Pass context.cdm_session_factory when constructing OmopGraphAdapter; Engine mode only works for colocated databases. context.cdm_engine is the primary-role engine and cannot query vocabulary on a split deployment.
  8. Use the current public error codes: LEGACY_REGISTRY, MISPLACED_REGISTRY, MISSING_STORAGE_TABLE, MODEL_REGISTRATION_CONFLICT, and READ_ONLY_STORE.
  9. Update describe() consumers for the llm_model, stack, groundworkers, and app_name keys and cdm_schema / vocab_schema names. The old base.sql schema/engine helpers have been removed; use oa-configurator's physical_schema_of, qualified, supports_schemas, and schema_for_role APIs.
  10. Update direct AppConfig construction for the required stack, groundworkers, cdm_database, cdm_engine, cdm_vocab_engine, cdm_session_factory, embedding_model, llm_model, vector_store, and knowledge_root fields; prefer build_app_config() in plugins and tests.

docs.title: Setup steps
docs.text:
Plugin data preparation belongs in registered setup steps. A plugin may expose a setup_steps tuple of PluginSetupStep instances. Each step declares a stable key, operator copy, typed arguments, and a build_plan(values, config_path) callable that returns a MaintenancePlan.

The host provides the common setup-console form and review flow, passes argument values only to that run, and starts the resulting plan through the durable maintenance-run store. Logs, progress, cancellation, retry, and the Runs view are therefore shared by core operations and plugins.

Setup arguments are separate from package configuration: database/model references and policy defaults belong in configuration, while paths to an input export belong to the one-off setup run.

Long-running plugin work should be represented by commands in the plan and run out of process. The command may invoke the plugin's own setup module or console entry point; Groundworkers does not import plugin internals or reproduce their loading logic.

docs.title: Readiness verification
docs.text:
A plugin may implement GroundworkersPluginReadiness.verify_readiness(state) when operators need to distinguish valid package configuration from an initialised, usable capability.

Verification is read-only and returns a PluginReadinessResult containing a stable state, a summary, and PluginReadinessField values. Display values must never contain credentials, connection URLs, or raw exception text.

The contract is headless: it contains no Groundskeeping types. Groundworkers uses the same result for generic setup-console rendering, while a plugin may return result.as_dict() from its own MCP status tool. Plugins own dependency- specific checks; the host only builds current plugin state, handles unavailable configuration safely, and maps readiness states to existing Groundskeeping status, table, empty, action, and detail contracts.

docs.title: Configuration linting
docs.text:
A plugin may implement the runtime-checkable GroundworkersPluginLinter protocol when its settings need checks beyond the configuration schema. The hook is lint_config(config) -> PluginLintReport; it receives the plugin's validated PackageConfigBase instance, or None when the plugin has no config class. It runs without calling build(), so it can check configuration-dependent files or cross-field rules without constructing runtime services.

Return a report with the plugin name and zero or more PluginLintDiagnostic values. Each finding has a stable code, error / warning / info severity, concise message, and optional configuration path. Errors make report.valid false; warnings and informational findings do not. Keep diagnostics safe for display: do not include secret values, full connection strings, or raw exception text.

Headless consumers call lint_plugin_config(plugin, config). It returns None when the optional protocol is not implemented. If a linter raises or returns a malformed report, Groundworkers logs a safe error summary and returns a generic error finding.

Run the installed plugin checks from the command line:

groundworkers lint-plugins --config-path /path/to/config.toml

The command prints a JSON report and exits with status 1 if any linter reports an error. Plugins without the optional hook appear under skipped; only plugins with the hook have their settings passed through their package schema and linter. It does not build the Groundworkers runtime or connect to OMOP services. This command covers plugin configuration only; prompt packs and Groundworkers knowledge packs should be validated by their owning subsystems.

docs.title: Lifecycle and diagnostics
docs.text: Groundworkers discovers the plugin set once per application build, validates its identities, resolves each package configuration, and builds state. MCP registration uses those same discovered objects. groundworkers --describe lists active plugins and safe plugin_issues for plugins skipped because their configuration, prerequisites, build, or registration failed.

docs.title: Proposal: per-domain standard-resolution packs
docs.text: Status: draft for review (2026-10-19). Replaces the single core/standard-concept-preference pack with a slim, always-loaded core plus one pack per OMOP domain.

docs.title: Why the broad pack falls short
docs.text:
standard-concept-preference mixes two kinds of content:

  1. Invariants that hold in every domain: the target must be standard_concept = 'S', active, never a classification ('C'), and concept_id = 0 when nothing fits.
  2. Per-domain resolution rules, compressed to one line each, e.g. "Procedure: SNOMED preferred, CPT4 for US billing".

The second kind is where agents actually go wrong, and one line per domain cannot carry it. Checking the procedure domain against the live vocabulary (v5.0 27-FEB-26) shows the one-liner is misleading:

  • Standardness is decided per code, not per vocabulary. CPT4 has ~10.2k standard codes and ~3.8k non-standard ones that map to SNOMED, CVX or RxNorm. OPCS4 and ICD9Proc are split roughly half and half.
  • A standard source code (CPT4, ICD10PCS, standard HCPCS) maps to itself. There is no "prefer SNOMED over CPT4" step: rewriting a standard code to SNOMED discards information and is wrong.
  • The vocabulary ships cross-vocabulary links that look like equivalences but aren't (CPT4 - SNOMED eq often points to a broader concept, or to several). An agent told only "prefer SNOMED" will follow them.
  • Concept sets built from SNOMED descendants miss standard CPT4/ICD10PCS records (e.g. CPT4 27447 total knee arthroplasty is not a descendant of SNOMED 43531648 Total knee replacement).

None of this applies to Condition, where one standard vocabulary (SNOMED) absorbs everything through Maps to. Each domain resolves to standardness differently, so each needs its own guidance.

docs.title: Proposed structure
docs.text:
packs/core/
  standard-concept-preference/      # KEEP name (always: true) — invariants only
  standard-resolution-condition/    # domains: [Condition]
  standard-resolution-procedure/    # domains: [Procedure]       ← drafted
  standard-resolution-measurement/  # domains: [Measurement]
  standard-resolution-observation/  # domains: [Observation]
  standard-resolution-drug/         # domains: [Drug]
  standard-resolution-device/       # domains: [Device]
  drug-concept-granularity/         # unchanged; see_also from -drug

The catalogue only discovers packs/<layer>/<pack>/manifest.yaml, so the domain packs are flat siblings rather than nested children. The link between them is see_also plus applicability.domains, which PackApplicability.matches() already filters on.

docs.title: Slim core: standard-concept-preference
docs.text:
Keep the name. It is always loaded and the bundled-baseline test asserts it exists (tests/unit/test_knowledge_catalogue.py:218). Contents:

  • Active-target rule. Follow Maps to from U; never target D.
  • S required for *_concept_id. C is never a target. Non-standard goes in *_source_concept_id.
  • New: standardness is per code. Check standard_concept on the concept, never infer it from vocabulary_id.
  • New: a standard source concept maps to itself. Do not re-map it to a "preferred" vocabulary.
  • New: Maps to is the only mapping edge. eq, cat, poss_eq and Is a are evidence, not mappings.
  • concept_id = 0 fallback.
  • Loading rule: "after resolving a target's domain_id, load standard-resolution-<domain>".
  • The vocab_preference block is removed and moves into the domain packs.

docs.title: Domain pack template
docs.text:
Every standard-resolution-<domain> pack uses the same sections, so an agent knows where to look:

Section Purpose 1. Standard vocabularies in this domain Which vocabularies hold S concepts here, and roughly what share. Snapshot counts carry a verified_against vocabulary version. 2. Resolution path by input type (a) code from a standard vocabulary, (b) non-standard code, (c) free text. Each has its own path. 3. Relationship semantics Which relationship_ids are mappings, which are evidence, and the known failure modes of each. 4. Concept-set implications Whether descendants of one vocabulary cover the others. If not, how to build a set that does. 5. Traps Concrete patterns the vocabulary gets wrong, with concept IDs. 6. Verification checklist What to check before accepting a target.

rules.yaml carries the machine-readable half under the same keys: standard_vocabularies, resolution_paths, relationship_semantics, concept_set_roots, traps, checks. Worked cases go in examples.yaml, which PackContent already loads.

docs.title: What each domain pack must cover (outline)
docs.text:
• Condition: SNOMED is the only standard vocabulary. ICD10CM/ICD9CM/ICD10 reach it via Maps to, sometimes 1:n (see one-to-many-mapping). Covers Maps to value for pre-coordinated codes (see pre-coordinated-split), Cancer Modifier / ICDO3 for oncology, and the domain-change trap (an ICD10CM code mapping into Observation).
  • Procedure: see the draft. Multiple standard vocabularies, self-maps, eq/cat semantics, attribute-based alignment, concept sets with several roots.
  • Measurement: LOINC and SNOMED are both standard. LOINC wins for lab tests. Covers CPT4 lab codes (1.3k standard CPT4 Measurement codes, plus CPT4 - LOINC eq) and the test+result split.
  • Observation: SNOMED / LOINC / CPT4 E&M / HCPCS. Covers history-of (see history-of-event) and E&M visit codes landing in Observation.
  • Drug: RxNorm before RxNorm Extension. Covers HCPCS J-codes and CPT4 vaccine/drug codes that are non-standard and map to RxNorm/CVX. Granularity is delegated to drug-concept-granularity.
  • Device: HCPCS Level II is the main standard source (5.2k S). Covers SNOMED physical objects and the Procedure/Device split for implant-plus-procedure codes.

docs.title: Mechanism note
docs.text: post-filter is declared in manifests, but nothing reads rules.yaml programmatically today. knowledge_pack only returns it in the payload (tools/knowledge_tools.py:189). The domain packs keep rules.yaml declarative so a future post-filter can use it. The guidance is written to stand on its own when it is context-injected.

docs.title: Migration
docs.text:
1. Land standard-resolution-procedure. It adds content and changes nothing existing.
  2. Draft the remaining domain packs from the template.
  3. Slim standard-concept-preference to the invariants and add the loading rule. Bump it to version: "2.0".
  4. Mirror into gw-plugins/kb-prompts/packs/core/, whose standard-concept-preference is currently byte-identical.

Dependency-shaped wrapper around the omop-graph backend runtime.

The read-oriented server builds the graph with write=False, and omop-graph derives its on-demand query encoder from the writer interface — so without a Groundworkers-supplied encoder the embedding resolver would run and return nothing. The backend is provider-neutral (any-llm), so this adapter holds no provider-specific behaviour and no HTTP client of its own. What it does own is the translation into Groundworkers' contracts: GroundworkersError codes instead of provider exceptions, and plain JSON-safe dicts for the MCP tool layer.

Two completion modes are available:

  • Text completion (complete_text): returns a raw text response.
  • Structured completion (complete_structured): requests a JSON response matching a caller-supplied schema. Preferred for MCP-facing tools where downstream agents need to parse the output reliably.

The schema is injected into the system prompt and JSON mode is requested from the provider. This is compatible with Ollama, vLLM, and OpenAI endpoints, and deliberately does not use omop-llm's extract(): that requires a Pydantic model and a provider that declares native structured output, whereas callers here supply a raw JSON schema.

The response is parsed but not validated against the schema — callers are responsible for validating the returned dict (e.g. with Pydantic).

Raises INVALID_INPUT if model_name names a different model or if response_schema is not JSON-serializable. Raises BACKEND_UNAVAIL if the call fails. Raises QUERY_ERROR if the response is not valid JSON.

Exposes raw quality signals (ts_rank, standard_concept flag) so callers can apply their own quality thresholds and decide whether to navigate non-standard results to their standard equivalents.

docs.title: GraphService

Accepts a batch of field labels and their example response values, and returns a mapping of label → OMOP domain string for any label that can be confidently classified. Labels that yield null or an unrecognised domain are omitted so that callers fall through to the next resolution tier (keyword heuristics).
